While it is generally not illegal to be nude in your own home, you can face indecent exposure charges if you are visible to the public. The specific laws and interpretation vary by location, but they focus on public exposure and the intent behind the nudity.

Public view: Being naked inside your home is typically legal as long as you maintain a reasonable expectation of privacy and are not intentionally exposing yourself to others. Problems can arise if your windows are uncovered and you can be easily seen from a public space, such as the street or a neighboring property.


Intent: The intent behind the nudity is a critical factor. You are more likely to face charges if a prosecutor can prove you intentionally exposed yourself to offend, annoy, or sexually gratify yourself or others. If you were unaware that you were visible, or if the exposure was an accident, it is less likely to be considered a crime.

Backyard nudity: Nudity in a private backyard is usually fine if it is shielded from public view by a tall fence or other barriers. However, if neighbors or passersby can easily see you, a complaint could lead to indecent exposure charges.

Children present: If children are involved, child welfare concerns may also be a factor. Most jurisdictions take a more serious view of any public nudity that might involve or affect minors.

Local variations: Laws can vary significantly by state, county, and municipality. Some areas have more relaxed views on nudity than others. What is permissible in one city may not be in another.

A small correction.

"We all know that the word assault means to be physically touched by somebody"

That's not accurate. Legally speaking, assault is actually what comes before physical contact. The physical contact itself is battery.

The three key elements of assault are: intent to cause the victim to fear imminent harmful or offensive contact, the victim's reasonable apprehension of such contact, and the immediacy of the perceived threat.

None of this should detract from this woman's ridiculous claims, but if we're going to discuss all this, we should make sure we actually understand the words we're using.

On a related note, it is generally held that an unconscious person cannot commit assault as a person who is unconscious lacks the capacity for intent and is not aware of their actions.

A few technical observations: There's a white storm door there that swings out to the right side of the video, and it has no door closer on it and it is left open. The lack of a door closer and the fact that it's left open in sweatshirt weather indicates a rather sloppy level of attention to details. Having the ceiling fan on in such weather also indicates the same, though ceiling fan switches are often located right next to the light switch, and both could have been turned on accidentally if someone were drunk. (On the other hand many ceiling fans are wired on the same switch as the light in the same fixture, with the fan controlled by a pull chain, and this being autumn, the resident(s) may have had the fan running through the summer, and forgotten to turn off the fan as the weather got cooler).
-- The storm door appears to be one of the thicker insulated types, and the outer door jamb appears to show some of that gray, stick-on foam weatherstripping. That foam weatherstripping needs to compress for the door to close, and if the door isn't installed carefully, it may not latch properly. And if it were a pain in the neck to get it to close properly, this may explain why it was left open.
-- The inner door, the main front door, would be up against the inner part of the door jamb if it were closed. This inner jamb is painted dark brown, and is scuffed fairly noticeably next to the dead-bolt striker plate. There are also some scuffs next to the knob-lock striker plate. Furthermore, most of the upper part of the inner door jamb is scuffed, along with a small spot down low. This front door takes some effort to close, but even if it doesn't latch, the friction of the door edge against the jamb would tend to hold it pretty much closed, unless there were a pretty good wind blowing. And there were no sighs of wind in the video (look at the woman's hair).
-- Many front doors these days come with compression gaskets around the jambs, and even when they are installed according to the manufacturer's instructions, they do not latch reliably, and if this were one of those doors, that would have made it more likely that the door in this case didn't latch properly and easily blew open. But there was no compression gasket on the inside door, so this explanation doesn't work. The door may not have latched properly, but it wouldn't have blown open because of all of the friction against the door jamb.
-- He may have left the door open intentionally, or she may have seen that it was ajar (almost closed, but a little bit open), and pushed it inward.
-- From the loose articles on the porch and the interior, the interior "decor," and the presence of another entry door to the right of this guy's door, I suspect that he's a moderately sloppy bachelor tenant in a duplex, and that's a demographic that tends to get intoxicated at times.
-- So I do NOT think that the door blew open, though it may well not have been latched. I think that either he left it open intentionally, or that she saw it ajar, and pushed it open. As for his situation on the couch, maybe he was drunk and thought he could rub one out before the food arrived and fell asleep. It may be relevant information whether this delivery arrived earlier than usual. As far as the "on purpose" accusation, it's my understanding, from the way such things are presented in media, that exposers like to observe the reactions of their victims. But then I don't grasp the motivation behind that sort of thing at all.

It seems unlikely that he left the door wide open, because it's sweatshirt weather, and the purposeful exposure explanation, without his being able to see her reaction seems even more unlikely than the drunken thought that he could rub one out before the food arrived and fell asleep.
